lawyer:
Obaidur Rahman Masala, Advocate ----- For the Petitioner. 
Abul Kalam  Mainuddin with Jahangir Alam, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Parties.
parties:
Zila Parishad, Chittagong ----- Petitioner 
Vs. 
Abdul Halim and others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: Defendant Zila Parishad, Chittagong obtained this Rule from the judgment and decree dated 21st May, 2003 of the Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Chittagong in Other Class Appeal No. 4 of 2003 affirming those dated 30th September 2002 of the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Chittagong in Other Class Suit No.8 of 1999.

2. Opposite party Nos. 1-8 instituted the suit for declaration of title by adverse possession in the suit property and for further declaration that the RS khatian and other corresponding khatians in respect of the suit lands were prepared in accordance with law.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that the suit lands along with other property belonged to Azmot Ali Khan Nayabad Taluk. Golam Gafur Sawdagor and Asgor Ali took settlement of the suit lands by registered deed dated 20th February, 1877. Previously the suit lands were used as tea garden but subsequently, the then Government gave possession of some lands in favour of Golam Gafur Sawdagor and thereafter, the Government took over possession of the remaining lands and handed over the same in favour of the Zila Parishad. Golam Gafur Sawdagor died leaving four sons, Kala Miah, Asmot Ali, Abdus Samad, Abdul Goni and daughters Ammajan and Mirujan. The lands were recorded in CS No. 130 kheyat khatian in their names. Kala Miah died unmarried and his other brother Abdul Gani got the suit lands exclusively by an amicable partition. Abdul Gani died before the preparation of the RS record and the lands were recorded in RS khatian No. 982 in the name of his son Noor Hossain. The defendant did not file any objection against the said record. Noor Hossain handed over possession of the said lands in favour of Moqbul Ahmed by deed dated 26th October 1944. Moqbul Ahmed thereafter transferred it in favour of Haji Fazor Rahman and Saleh Ahmed Sowdagor by kabala dated 14th April 1948. Saleh Ahmed thereafter by kabalas dated 2nd October 1954 and 12th October 1954 transferred his share in favour of Abdul Monaf Contractor. The RS record was also prepared in his name. Abdul Monaf developed the suit lands, raised semipucca structures thereon and rented the said houses to the tenants. A Municipality holding was prepared in the name of the plaintiffs' predecessor. After the death of Abdul Monaf Contractor, the plaintiffs inherited the suit lands. The further case of the plaintiffs is that though the Zila Parishad's right to realise rent from the plaintiffs was extinguished, it served a notice upon them which clouded their title in the suit lands. The plaintiffs failed to obtain proper reliefs in Other Class Suit No. 95 of 1992 as they sought irrelevant reliefs in that suit. The Zila Parishad gained over the tenants of the plaintiffs who denied the plaintiffs' title, for which, the plaintiffs were compelled to institute the suit.

4. The case of the defendant, in short, is that the plaintiffs have not acquired any title on the strength of deed dated 20th February 1877, that the said deed does not attract the suit lands and that without a local investigation it is not possible to ascertain whether the suit lands appertain to RS khatian No. 982. Its further case was that the RS record was wrongly prepared in the name of the plaintiffs predecessor. The suit lands belonged to the Zila Parishad under the Government. The plaintiff's predecessor in collusion with the corrupt staffs of the Zila Parishad got the suit lands recorded in his name in RS khatian No. 982 as possessor in the remark column. Zila Parishad did not settle the suit lands in favour of Noor Hossain. The plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 95 of 1992 in respect of the suit lands and they lost in First Appeal No. 39 of 1995 in the High Court Division, and in the Appellate Division and thus, the suit is hit by the principles of res judicata and therefore, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

5. The learned Joint District Judge on consideration of the evidence on record by judgment and order dated 28th May 2003 decreed the suit. On appeal by the petitioner, being Other Class Appeal No.4 of 2003, the learned Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Chittagong who heard the said appeal by judgment and order dated 21st May, 2003 dismissed the appeal and maintained those of the trial Court.

6. Mr Md Obaidur Rahman Mostafa, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, argues that admittedly the plaintiffs have failed to establish their title by adverse possessions in the suit lands up to the Appellate Division and that the Courts below on a misreading of the judgments, Exhibits B and B (1), have erroneously held that the suit was not barred by res judicata. In this connection, the learned Advocate has taken us to the plaints and the judgments.

7. On a plain reading of the plaint, we find inconsistent claim of the plaintiffs in the suit lands. Initially, they made averments in paragraph 1(one) of the plaint stating that "১নং বিবাদী ৮.২৮ একরের মধ্যে ৭.৭০ একর জমি নিজ খাস দখলে রাখিয়া ৫৮ শতক আব্দুল গনির পুত্র নুর হোসেন নামক ব্যক্তির বরাবরে ১১। ৩(১১ আনা তিন পাই) খাজনা ধার্য্যে লগিয়ত করেন” After institution of the suit, they filed an application for amendment of the plaint and the prayer was allowed on 11th May, 2002. In the said amendment they inserted one paragraph at the top as paragraph No. 1 one and the original paragraph No.1(one) has been numbered as 1(ka). By way of amendment, they have introduced a new story about the plaintiffs acquisition of title in the suit lands stating that the suit lands along with other properties belonged to Azmat Ali Kha Taluk, that the plaintiffs' predecessors Golam Gafur Sowdagar and Asgor Ali took settlement by registered deed dated 13th Magh, 1238 BS and that the settlement holders had tea plantations thereon. Thereafter they claimed "পরবর্তীক্রমে তদানিন্তন সরকার বাহাদুর উক্ত সম্পত্তির মধ্যে কতেক সম্পত্তি বাদীগনের পূর্ববর্তী গোলাম গফুর সওদাগর খাস দখলের প্রদান পূর্বক বাকী সম্পত্তি অতিরিক্ত সম্পত্তি হওয়ার কারনে তাহা সরকার বাহাদুর গ্রহন ক্রমে সরকারের আয় বৃদ্ধি কল্পে ১নং বিবাদীর দপ্তর পরিচালনার নিমিত্তে তাবৎ সম্পত্তির শাসন সংরক্ষনের ভার ১নং বিবাদীর উপর ন্যাস্ত করিলে.............................।

However, they have not changed the averments made in original paragraph No. 1 about their acquisition of title and allowed the same to remain in paragraph 1(ka).

8. Plaintiffs now claim that by way of settlement and successive transfers from the Azmot Ali Kha taluk they have acquired title in the suit lands. On the other hand, they claimed that the then Government handed over some lands in favour of Golam Gafur Sawdagor. If the suit lands were settled to Golam Gafur and Asgor Ali by registered deed, how the Government gave possession of some lands out of the said lands to Golam Gofur again is not clear to us? It is also not clear to us how the Government has taken over possession of the remaining lands and handed over possession of additional lands to Zila Parishad? The plea of taking over lands as excess is an absurd story in that, before the promulgation of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (SA & T Act) there was no law authorising the Government to take over possession of lands from any individual as excess lands other than by way of acquisition. All rent receiving interests of persons who have been described as rent receivers in clause (23) of section 3 of SA & Act, i.e., rent receiving interests of (i) proprietors (ii) tenure holders (iii) raiyats, (iv) under-raiyats (v) non-agricultural tenants in some cases, (vi) landlords in respect of service tenures (vii) lands in khas possession of rent receivers (viii) hat or bazar, (ix) fishery and (x) forest, etc. have been acquired on and from the date of publication of Gazette Notification dated 14th April, 1956. Admittedly, the suit lands had been recorded in the RS Khatian No. 981 in the name of the Zila Parishad and thus the lands vested in the defendant prior to 1950. Plaintiffs claim that the defendant petitioner has settled 0.58 acres of land out of 8.28 acres of land to Noor Hossain and, on the other hand, they have claimed proprietary right in the said lands, which claims are self contradictory. This inconsistency has cropped up after introducing the story of settlement by Exhibit 1 in order to avoid the plea of res judicata.

9. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-opposite parties, fails to explain the' basis of the plaintiffs' title in the suit lands as pleaded in paragraphs 1 and 1(ka) of the plaint. The learned Advocate frankly concedes that there is some inconsistency in the pleadings about the acquisition of title in the suit lands but, according to the learned Advocate, this inconsistency will not stand in the way of plaintiffs getting decree in the suit since the RS Khatian No. 982 has been prepared in the name of plaintiff's predecessor. We find no force in the contention of the learned Advocate.

10. Pleadings must be drafted with sufficient definiteness to enable the opponent to understand the case he is called upon to meet. A plaint is the foundation of the suit although the statements in the plaint are not themselves evidence, the Court is required to see the statements in the plaint to ascertain what is the case of the plaintiff and draw reasonable inference after considering the same. We are of the view that a party cannot be allowed to charge his case or set up a case inconsistent with what he has stated in his pleadings. A party may take inconsistent pleas in the alternative such as, the plaintiff Can plead the right of ownership as well as the right to easement, but if he pleads ownership and fails, he cannot subsequently turn around and claim the right as an easement by prescription. A party who has inconsistent contentions to make must raise them by way of alternative contentions. He cannot be allowed to raise contentions piecemeal raising one after the other. The suit is liable to be dismissed on this ground alone but the Courts below have overlooked this inconsistency in the plaintiffs' claim in the suit lands.

11. On a close look into the deed dated 13th Magh 1238 BS corresponding to 20th February 1877, with naked eyes, it will not be difficult to detect, even by a layman, over writings in various parts and use of separate inks and insertion of a few sentences with different inks at the bottom of the deed. The learned Advocate submits that as the document is very old one the words which were indistinct were overwritten for the purpose of understanding the recital in it. We failed to understand how a registered deed could have been made readable by overwriting by the party in whose favour it was filed? If there was existence of such registered deed, the plaintiffs could have obtained a certified copy thereof and filed the original along with the certified copy for the inspection of the Court. We have no hesitation to hold that this deed is a spurious document and that the Courts below have overlooked the over writings and interpolations in it. Besides that, there is no material on record to show that this deed attracts the suit lands. There is also no legal evidence to show that CS 130 kheyat khatian corresponds to RS plot No. 982 as claimed by the plaintiffs. The defendant has challenged this deed on the ground that the said deed does not attract the suit lands but the plaintiffs have not taken steps for relayment of the deed by way of local investigation. The trial Court answered the objection in the following manner:

"আরজির তপসিল বর্নিত বিরোধীয় সি,এস, খতিয়ান ও দাগের সম্পত্তি যে আর,এস, জরিপে বিরোধীয় আর, এস, নং ৯৮২ খতিয়ান ও দাগের অন্তর্ভূক্ত হয়ে রেকর্ড হয়েছে তা প্রমান করার জন্য বাদী পক্ষ সি, এস, ও আর, এস, দাগের নকসা অনুসারে super imposition পদ্ধতির মাধ্যমে সার্ভে জানা একজন বিজ্ঞ এ্যাডভোকেট জনাব সাখাওয়াত হোসেন চৌধুরী কর্তৃক trace map দাখিল করেছেন যা প্রদর্শনী ১৪ হিসাবে চিহ্নিত হইয়াছে। উক্ত প্রদর্শণী ১৪ দেখা যায় যে, আরজির তপসিল বর্নিত বিরোধীয় সি,এস,খতিয়ান ও দাগের সম্পত্তি বিরোধীয় আর,এস, ৯৮২ নং খতিয়ান ভুক্ত প্রদর্শনী ২(ক)."

12. How fallacious the observations of the trial Court are? We are shocked to notice these observations, which are apparently based upon inadmissible evidence. The plaintiffs have not examined this Shakhawat Hossain Chowdhury in the suit and he has not relayed the suit lands with Exhibit 1. Under such circumstances, how the alleged trace map prepared by said Shakhawat Hossain Chowdhury in connection with other purposes could be used as legal evidence in this suit and a decision was given holding that the said deed of 1877 attracted the CS khatian No. 130 and the RS khatian No. 982 as claimed by the plaintiffs? The plaintiffs instead of filing the original CS khatian, filed the certified copies as Exhibits 2 and 2(ka). These certified copies were obtained on 28th July, 2002 after institution of the suit just after amendment of the plaint. We find over writings in column 11 and therefore, it cannot be said to be an exaggeration if we hold that the plaintiffs cooked up a story by procuring the deed of 1877 and the CS khatian which do not relate to the suit lands after failing to establish their title in the earlier suit with a view to grab the suit lands.

13. The Courts below upon superficial consideration of these documents held, that the plaintiffs' had acquired title by adverse possession in the suit lands over 100 years by flouting the findings of this Court and the Appellate Division. This claim of acquisition of title on the basis of Exhibits 1 and 2 series is inconsistent with their claim made in paragraph 1(Ka) to the plaint. This inconsistency disproves the plaintiffs' acquisition of title in the suit lands. The Courts below overlooked these contradictory versions of the plaintiffs' claim in the suit lands and held that since the issues involved in the earlier suit were not identical with the issues involved in this suit, the suit was not barred by principle of res judicata. We hold that these findings of the Courts below are based upon misreading, non-consideration and superficial consideration of the evidence on record.

14. Admittedly, the plaintiffs instituted Other Class Suit No. 95/92-157/94 in respect of the suit lands in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong. The suit was decreed on 29th January, 1995. The petitioner preferred FA No. 39 of 1995 in this Court and this Court by judgment and order dated 22nd January, 1998 (Exhibit B) allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. Petitioner thereupon preferred Civil Petition No. 447 of 1998 in the Appellate Division. The Appellate Division by judgment and order dated 1st June, 1998(Exhibit B1) rejected the Leave Petition summarily. Thereafter, the plaintiffs instituted this present suit on 1st February, 1999 after about 8(eight) months of the rejection of the Leave Petition. In paragraph 5 of the plaint, the plaintiffs explained the cause for filing this suit over the same subject matter after losing up to the Appellate Division to the effect that "বাদীগন অগত্যা অনন্যোপায় হইয়া স্বত্বের মোকদ্দমা করে। তাড়াহুড়া করিয়া মামলা দায়েরের ফলে এবং উপযুক্ত ও প্রকৃত ও আইনানুগ পরামর্শের অভাবে বাদীগন তাহাদের দায়েরী মামলার আর্জি সঠিকভাবে গঠন করিতে ব্যর্থ হন” This averment proved that the plaintiffs instituted a suit in respect of the suit lands being Other Class Suit No. 95 of 1992. Despite this admitted position, the Court of appeal below observed that in the absence of the judgment and decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 95 of 1992, it could be ascertained who were the plaintiffs in that suit and the area of lands involved in that suit. The trial Court, on the other hand, observed that in the absence of the plaint and judgment and decree of the trial Court, it was not comprehensible about the nature and the issues involved in that suit. These observations are in utter misreading of the plaint and Exhibits Band B(1).

15. In the judgment (Exhibit B), this Court observed that the plaintiffs instituted the said suit in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Chittagong against the defendant-appellant (petitioner) praying for "declaration of their title and possession over the suit land." The petitioners by way of supplementary affidavit filed the plaint of Other Suit No. 95 of 1992 and the judgment of the trial Court. On perusal of the judgment, we find that the learned Joint District Judge has framed five issues and the issue No.5 reads as follows: "নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে বাদী পক্ষে স্বত্ত্ব দখল আছে কি নাঃ The learned Joint District Judge decreed the suit declaring "নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে বাদী পক্ষের স্বত্ত্ব স্বার্থ,  অধিকার ও দখল আছে মর্মে ঘোষিত হয়” The defendant- petitioner's resisted this suit on the plea of res judicata. The Courts below for reasons not known to us in order to avoid this plea not only misread the pleadings and the evidence on record, but also made inconsistent observations. The plaintiffs themselves admitted that they had instituted a suit earlier in respect of the suit lands and lost up to the Appellate Division. Therefore, there is no dispute that they were the plaintiffs in the earlier suit. The decree in FA No. 39 of 1995 (Exhibit B) clearly shows that the plaintiffs instituted the earlier suit.

16. Mr Khan submits that in the earlier suit the plaintiffs prayed for simple declaration without seeking title in the suit lands, and as the reliefs in both the suits are not distinct, this suit is not barred by res judicata. "There is no dispute that the defendant No.1 was the owner of the suit land and that the RS khatian No. 981 was accordingly, prepared in the name of the defendant No. 1. The plaintiffs-respondents claimed their title and possession over the suit land on the basis of the preparation of RS khatian in the name of Noor Hossain under superior landlord, the defendant No. 1 i.e. the District Council, in which he was in possession after taking settlement. Exhibit No.1 is the certified copy of the RS khatian of the suit land. It appears that this khadail was prepared in the name of the defendant No.1, the District Council, and under this khatian a sub-khatian being No. 982 was prepared in the name of Noor Hossain showing his possession in the remark column without describing his status either as raiyat or a sub-lessee though a jama of Taka 11 annas 8 and 3 pie are noted in this khatian in column meant for rent." The High Court Division observed in Exhibit B. "It is the definite case of the plaintiffs respondents that Noor Hossain was the owner in possession of the suit land in raiyati right under the defendant No. 1 i.e. the District Council. But the plaintiffs-respondents could not file any paper to show the alleged raiyati right of No or Hossain either on the basis of settlement or lease taken from the defendant No. 1 i.e. the District Council. Further, plaintiffs respondents could not file any rent receipt to show that Noor Hossain ever paid rent of the suit land to the defendant No. 1 i.e. the District Council or that the District Council ever realised any rent from Noor Hossain."

17. The Appellate Division in Civil Petition No. 457 of 1998 (Exhibit B1) observed as follows:

"True but the plaintiffs could not file any paper to show the alleged raiyati right of Nur Hossain on the basis of settlement or lease taken from defendant No.1. The High Court Division was well founded in law in holding that under the circumstances the plaintiffs have established a case of possession but not title. When they are in possession claiming raiyati settlement they cannot set up adverse possession either. They are not entitled to a declaration of title".

18. In view of the above findings and the admission of the plaintiffs in the plaint about the dismissal of their earlier suit over the same subject matter, two vital questions are involved in this Rule, one, whether the suit is barred by the principle of res judicata, and whether, even after losing in the earlier suit, the plaintiffs can avoid the plea of res judicata by introducing new facts, which they failed to produce in the earlier suit.

19. Mr TH Khan, learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-opposite parties, contends that a plea of res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law and a litigant, who is raising the said plea has to prove the said plea of adducing evidence. He argues that the defendant-petitioner has not filed the plaint and the judgment of the trial Court to show that the issues involved in the earlier suit and this suit are identical. Mr Khan contended that the findings of this Court in the earlier suit and the Appellate Division were erroneous since the suit lands were basically agricultural lands, after the SA&T Act came into force, the raiyats became maliks and therefore, the plaintiffs' possession in the suit lands had matured into title. It is further argued that since the earlier findings are based upon erroneous decision, the question of res judicata does not arise in this suit. In support of his contention Mr Khan has referred the case of Chairman, Chingleput Municipality vs M Murugesa Mudaliar and others, AlR 1933(Madras) 59.

20. In the said reported case, it was observed: "Erroneous decision on a question of law in a previous suit would not be a bar in a subsequent suit between the same parties, and a different decision may be given on that question but the decisions given should not in any way affect the operation of the former decree or take away any right of the party thereunder". We fail to understand why Mr Khan has referred this decision? In the earlier suit no issue was raised or framed to consider whether the suit lands were agricultural or non-agricultural. Accordingly, no decision was given in that regard. In this suit also no issue was framed or suggested by the plaintiffs on this point. The plaintiffs are raising the point for the first time in revision and we are, therefore, not prepared to give any observation at this stage. The plaintiffs did not claim that the earlier suit was instituted in a Court which had no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon it and thus, all findings and decisions given in that suit were without jurisdiction. Mr Khan seeks to equate an incorrect decision with a decision rendered without jurisdiction. It has been observed in State of West Bengal vs Hemant Kumar, AIR 1966 SC 1061.

"A wrong decision by a Court having jurisdiction is as much binding between the parties as a right one and may be superseded by appeals to higher tribunals or other procedure like review which law provides."

21. Mr Khan has referred the case of Mathura Prasad Sarjoo Jaiswal vs Dossibai NB Jeejeebhoy, AIR 1971 (SC) 2355. In the reported case, the Supreme Court observed as follows:

"A question relating to the jurisdiction of a Court cannot be deemed to have been finally determined by an erroneous decision of the Court. If by an erroneous interpretation of the statute the Court holds that it has no jurisdiction, the question would not, in our judgment, operate as res judicata. Similarly, by an erroneous decision if the Court assumes jurisdiction which it does not possess under the statute the question cannot operate as res judicata between the same parties, whether the cause of action in the subsequent litigation is the same or otherwise".

22. In the above reported case, the question involved was, whether the decision of the civil judge affirmed by the Bombay High Court rejecting Mathura Prashad's application for fixation of standard rent under the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947 is res judicata in a fresh petition in the Court of Small Causes, Bombay for an order determining standard rent of the premises. In the facts of the given case, the Supreme Court was of the view that in determining the application of the rule of res judicata the Court is not concerned with the correctness or otherwise of the earlier judgment. The matter in issue, if it is one purely of fact, decided in the earlier proceeding by a competent Court, must in a subsequent suit between the same parties be regarded as finally decided and cannot be reopened. A mixed question of law and fact determined in the earlier proceeding between the same parties may not, for the same reason, be questioned in a subsequent proceeding between the same parties where the decision is on a question of interpretation of a statute, it will be res judicata in a subsequent proceeding. Therefore, this decision does not support plaintiffs' case. In Satyadhyan Ghosal vs Smt Deorajin Debi AlR 1960 (SC) 941, the Supreme Court observed:

"The principle of res judicata is based on the need of giving a finality to judicial decisions. What it says is that once a res judicata, it shall not be adjudged again. Primarily, it applies as between past litigation and future litigation. When a matter whether on a question of fact or a question of law has been decided between two parties in one suit or proceeding and the decision is final, either because no appeal was taken to a higher Court or because the appeal was dismissed, or no appeal lies, neither party will be allowed in a future suit or proceeding between the same parties to canvass the matter again. This principle of res judicata is embodied in relation to suits in section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure; but even where section 11 does not apply, the principle of res judicata has been applied by Courts for the purpose of achieving finality in litigation. The result of this is that the original Court as well as any higher Court must in any future litigation proceed on the basis that the previous decision was correct."

23. If the Court had no jurisdiction over a subject matter the decision of the Court is not res judicata in a subsequent suit. Mr Khan submits that since the issues involved in the earlier suit are not directly in issue in this suit, the decision in the earlier suit is not res judicata and, in support of his contention, he has referred the case of Durga Prasad Sharma vs Sadasib Biswal, AIR 1969 (Orissa),171. We do not dispute the proposition of law stated in that decision but in the earlier suit the plaintiffs claimed declaration of title and confirmation of possession and in this suit also they claimed similar reliefs besides other reliefs. The substantive relief in both the suits are for declaration of title and confirmation of possession in the suit lands.

24. We fully agree that a plea of res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law, and the party raising the plea has to be proved the same but in this case, the plaintiffs have admitted in their pleadings about the existence of decisions of the superior Courts over the same subject matter and between the same parties. In Mathura Prashad Sarjoo Jaiswal's case, the Supreme Court answered the said point observing, that a plea of res judicata is a mixed question of fact and law. Even a decision on a mixed question of law and fact is as much res judicata as one on a question of law. In Tarant Charan vs Kedar Nath AIR 1928 Calcutta (FB) 777, the Full Bench observed:

"In these circumstances, it matters nothing whether the decision was right or wrong and it matters nothing whether the error, if any, was an error on a point of fact or on a point of law. The matter directly and substantially in issue was a sensible and concrete question as to the rights of the parties .and the conditions and terms of the defendant's tenancy. To decide it correctly it was necessary to find the facts and to apply the law. If the Munsif did not succeed in ascertaining the exact facts or in applying the law correctly, the remedy of the defendant, if he had a remedy, was to challenge the Munsif's decision in a superior Court. But section 11, CPC and the principle which it embodies would be brought to nothing if it were held that it was open to him to litigate again the question of the validity of the terms as to interest, or his obligation to comply with it".

<u>25. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been incorporated in the Code for the purpose of convenience of the parties that any issue which has been decided between the parties over the same subject matter cannot be reopened between the parties or between parties under whom they or any of them claim, litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit. If at the time of decision of the earlier suit the facts which have been raised in the subsequent suit were available to the plaintiffs, their remedy, in our view, lies by way of filing a review petition under Order XLVII, CPC but they cannot be allowed to file a fresh suit on the same subject matter with new facts. New pleas of different terms on the same facts cannot be entertained.</u>

26. Even the subject matter of two suits may be different, the object of the suits, the reliefs and the causes of action may be different, but if the matter in issue in them is identical i.e. if the same title had been litigated before, res judicata will apply. A matter in issue between the parties is the right claimed by one party and denied by the other, and the claim of right from its very nature depends upon proof of facts and application of relevant law. The words "directly and substantially in issue" means if the matter was in issue directly in an earlier litigation and decided against a party then the decision would be res judicata in a subsequent proceeding.

<u>27. A wrong decision by a Court having jurisdiction is, as such, binding between parties as a right one. A judgment which is erroneous in fact or law is, nevertheless, res judicata so long as it is not vacated or rescinded or reversed by a Superior Court. An incorrect decision on a question of law cannot be equated with a decision passed without jurisdiction. Doctrine of res judicata covers adjudication both on factual and legal matters.</u>

28. In Mirza Mohammad vs. Chief Settlement Commissioner. Lahore, 17 DLR (SC) 105, the writ petitioner Md. Yakub filed a writ petition in the High Court of West Pakistan alleging that he was an allottee of the mill and that he had also spent a sum of Rs. 40,000 in respect of repairs and praying that the auction be stopped and the mill be transferred to him. The writ petition was dismissed. The petitioner then filed a review petition. The review petition was "dismissed on the grounds that the matter was entirely in the hands of the" Chief Settlement Commissioner who could grant or withhold sanction. Petitioner thereupon filed no appeal against the said order. Again he filed another writ petition stating that he had applied for sanction of the expenses incurred and the Engineer in charge had made a report in his favour, but the Chief Settlement Commissioner was, not transferring the property to him. This petition was dismissed. A Letters Patent Appeal was filed which was also dismissed on the ground that sanction of the Rehabilitation Authority for incurring expenditure had not been obtained. A review petition was also unsuccessfully moved against the said order. In the facts of the given case, the Supreme Court observed:

"a petitioner is not entitled to make different pleas at different times so as to file more than one writ petition on the same facts. For a further plea the proper course would be to file a petition for review if such petition was maintainable. The general principle of res judicata is applicable in the writ petition also".

29. It is not open for any Court except the one reviewing such order having jurisdiction to do so in appropriate proceedings to sit over the judgments of the Courts by sidelining it on the ground that the Court has not given its finding after considering the same on merit. Whether the Court has arrived at the finding rightly or wrongly, if it has attained the finality, it is binding on the parties, and the parties cannot resile from it; and in the subsequent proceedings, the authority or Court before whom any proceeding takes place have also to treat those findings as binding on the parties and give effect to it.

30. The principle of res judicata operates on the Court. It is the Court which is prohibited from trying the issue which was directly and substantially in issue in the earlier suit between the parties provided the Court trying the subsequent proceeding is satisfied that the earlier Court was competent to dispose of the suit and that the suit had been heard and finally decided by that Court. The principle of res judicata is based on the need of giving a finality to judicial decisions. The matter which prevents the same case being tried twice litigated is of general application and is not limited by the specific words of section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Res judicata applies also as between two stages in the same litigation to the extent that a Court, whether the trial Court or the higher Court having at an earlier stage decided a matter in one way will not allow the parties to reagitate the matter again at a subsequent stage of the same proceedings. The provisions of section 11 are mandatory and a litigant can avoid the provisions by taking advantage of section 44 of the Evidence Act, which defines with precision the grounds of such avoidance as fraud or collusion. The plaintiffs did not raise any plea of fraud or collusion in paragraph 5 of the plaint. They pleaded that while drawing up the plaint hurriedly, they failed to bring material facts and law in the plaint. This is not a legal ground for avoiding decisions given by proper Court having jurisdiction to try the suit. The plaintiff-opposite parties did not claim that the earlier Court had no jurisdiction to determine the issues involved in the suit as framed. The plaintiffs failed to establish their title by adverse possession in the suit lands in the earlier suit.

31. Even if it is assumed that the plaintiff hurriedly instituted the suit but after institution of the suit, they got sufficient time to amend the plaint. They did not amend the plaint and allowed it to dispose of finally. Even after institution of this suit on 1st February, 1999, they did not bring those facts of acquisition of title in the suit lands. They included those facts by way of amendment of the plaint on 11th May, 2002, after 3-1/2 years of the date of institution of the suit by bringing completely a new story. They did not amend the original claim made in paragraph 1 of the plaint, now in paragraph 1(ka), which averments are inconsistent with them.

32. Mr Khan submits that since both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiffs are in possession over 100 years relying upon the deed dated 20th February, 1877 Exhibit 1, this finding cannot be disturbed in exercise of revisional jurisdiction. It is unfortunate to note that the Courts below flagrantly flouted the findings of this Court and the Appellate Division and declared plaintiffs' title by adverse possession in the suit lands. We do not dispute that the concurrent findings of the Courts below are immune from interference by this Court in exercising revisional jurisdiction but if the concurrent findings are based upon misreading or non-consideration of the evidence or other materials on record or it has been founded on misconception or misapplication of law or on misinterpretation of a document or otherwise it is perverse, there is no legal bar to interfere with the concurrent findings. We find no substance in the contention of Mr Khan. Mr Khan finally submits that since there are concurrent findings, the matter should be remanded to the trial Court for enabling the plaintiffs an opportunity to relay Exhibit 1 by way of local investigation. As we observed that Exhibit 1 was a spurious document, we consider it unnecessary to remand the case for local investigation and so further prolong this ruinously protracted litigation because, in our view, the question of title in the suit lands was directly and substantially in issue between the plaintiffs and the defendant in the earlier suit and decided against the plaintiffs.

33. Since this Court and the Appellate Division clearly found that the plaintiffs failed to establish their title in the suit lands, we cannot sit over those judgments and decide whether or not those decisions were illegal or erroneous. The suit is apparently barred under section 11, CPC and therefore, the same is liable to be dismissed. The Courts below, on a misconception of law and fact, held that the suit was not barred by the principle of res judicata. The suit is not legally maintainable and the judgments of the Courts below are liable to be interfered with. We find merit in this Rule.

34. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with costs. The impugned judgments are hereby set aside and the suit is dismissed.

Send down the lower Court records.

End.
